findings.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches addresses with a case-sensitive SQL equality (BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first), so a blocked address is bypassed simply by typing the same address with different capitalization (e.g. BAD@SpamClub.com when bad@spamclub.com is stored). Discourse runs on Postgres where text equality is case-sensitive and nothing in the 2013-era signup path normalizes email case, so a spammer whose address is blocked re-registers by capitalizing one letter: the blocked check misses, match_count/last_match_at never record the attempt, and the feature this PR exists to deliver fails against the easiest adversarial input — even though the same validator's domain whitelist/blacklist check is deliberately case-insensitive (Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)), making the exact-match gap unintended.

[ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, rake task, seed file, or API endpoint creates rows — so the only production write path is a hand-written SQL INSERT. Site staff without database access cannot block an email address from the application at all, the blocked-email validation added to every signup stays permanently dormant until someone manually loads the table, and each signup still pays the extra SELECT against a table that is empty by construction on any deploy made expecting this feature to work.

[ADVISORY] The new failure-payload fields (errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: user.attributes.slice(...)) that the client's rejectedEmails state machine consumes are introduced with no test anywhere in the diff asserting this response contract. A later refactor that renames or drops these keys, or a Rails upgrade change in how ActiveModel::Errors serializes (Errors stopped being a Hash subclass in later Rails), breaks the client-side blocked-email feedback silently — the signup form stops pre-flagging rejected emails and users see only the generic flash message, with no failing spec to catch the regression.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches the submitted address with a case-sensitive exact-string lookup (BlockedEmail.where(email: email), line 12) and nothing on the signup path normalizes case, so a blocked address is bypassed simply by capitalizing it. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spamclub.com' registers successfully as 'Bad@SpamClub.com' — Postgres string comparison is case-sensitive and nothing downcases the input, so no BlockedEmail row is found and the account is created; the client-side rejectedEmails.contains check is likewise case-sensitive so not even an inline error appears, while the sibling domain-blacklist check on the same path (Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)) is deliberately case-insensitive, meaning the two email gates on one path disagree about case and match_count/last_match_at stay blind to every evasion.

[ADVISORY] The email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist enforcement this diff moves out of User#email_validator into EmailValidator (lines 4-12) has zero test coverage in the diff — spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the only validator spec added, stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and exercises only the blocked branch (spec lines 10-22), never setting either SiteSetting. A regression introduced by the move — e.g. the gsub/Regexp construction on lines 19-21 building the wrong domain pattern — ships with a green suite; sites relying on email_domains_blacklist or email_domains_whitelist silently stop filtering providers (or start rejecting every address) with no failing spec anywhere in this diff.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff verifies the new server-to-client contract the feature hangs on — UsersController#create emitting errors: user.errors.to_hash and values: user.attributes.slice(...) (lines 198-199) and the client pushing result.values.email into rejectedEmails (create_account_controller.js:273-275); the only specs added call validate_each in isolation with should_block? stubbed plus BlockedEmail model internals. The PR's acceptance behavior — a signup with a blocked email fails, the response carries errors.email and values.email, and the field then shows inline rejection — is asserted nowhere, so any drift in the response shape (a rename, or the rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid branch returning without the new keys) silently disables the client-side rejectedEmails flow with zero test signal.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships BlockedEmail with a reader (should_block?) but no writer anywhere — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or user-block/deletion hook creates blocked_emails rows; the only creation code in the entire diff is the spec fabricator. The enforcement this PR builds stays dormant in every deployment until staff perform out-of-band SQL inserts — the diff's own spec comment acknowledges the workflow is 'manually load the table' (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:13-14) — so operators get no supported path to actually block an email address through the product.

[ADVISORY] The migration declares action_type NOT NULL with no default while the default lives only in the model's before_validation :set_defaults, so rows created outside the model — exactly the manual-loading path the diff's own spec comment documents — cannot be inserted. An operator following the blessed workflow hits 'null value in column "action_type" violates not-null constraint' on a plain INSERT INTO blocked_emails (email) VALUES (...), and one who guesses action_type: 0 inserts rows that silently never block — Discourse's Enum is 1-based (block=1, do_nothing=2), so should_block? returns false for 0 and the blocklist becomes a silent no-op.

[ADVISORY] The client consumes the new server error payload only as a boolean and renders the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for every rejectedEmails entry, discarding the specific per-cause message ('user.email.blocked' / 'is not allowed.', taken, domain-restricted) that result.errors.email actually carries. A user whose address is permanently blocked sees the same generic 'invalid email' inline message as a user with a typo (the specific reason surfaces only once in the transient flash), so they cannot distinguish a fixable mistake from a permanent ban and keep retrying the exact address the server just rejected.

[BUG] The client pushes the submitted email into rejectedEmails whenever the server response contains ANY email error — including uniqueness ("has already been taken") and domain-restriction ("not_allowed") errors — not just blocked-email errors, so the permanent-rejection behavior is not traceable to the blocked-users requirement it ships under. A returning user who enters an already-registered email (the single most common email error) gets the flash message once and then the inline field permanently reports the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') ("is invalid") for the rest of the session, replacing the server's actual reason; since the controller is a singleton the stale 'invalid' verdict persists across modal reopens.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships the blocked_emails table, model, migration, validator hook, and client pipeline with no writer anywhere — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed creates a BlockedEmail record. Operators cannot populate the blocklist through any product surface (the spec comment confirms the intended workflow is out-of-band manual SQL loads), so the feature is inert in production — every signup runs a lookup against a permanently empty table and the whole server+client+DB pipeline delivers nothing until follow-up code ships.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches with a case-sensitive exact lookup (where(email: email)) while the emails users type are never normalized to a canonical case, so the invariant 'blocked emails cannot register' is not enforced across case variants. A blocklist entry 'bad@spamclub.com' is trivially evaded by registering 'Bad@spamclub.com' (the unique index on blocked_emails.email is equally case-sensitive, so the two are distinct rows), defeating the spam-defense purpose of the feature with a one-character change.

[ADVISORY] should_block? mutates the database (match_count += 1, last_match_at, record.save) as a side effect of being invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, i.e., inside User model validation. Any code path that runs validation without a final save (valid?/errors probes, multi-step flows) records phantom match attempts and double-counts, and concurrent signup attempts lose increments through the read-modify-write update, so the match_count/last_match_at statistics — the observability the spec comment names as the feature's purpose ('we can see whether those emails have ever been blocked') — undercount and mislead the operator reading them; a save failure inside the predicate is also silently swallowed.

[ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction logic moved out of user.rb into this new validator has zero test coverage in the diff — the only spec (email_validator_spec.rb) stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and runs with blank SiteSettings, so neither restriction branch nor email_in_restriction_setting? (including the gsub('.', '\.') escaping and the changed self.email-to-value parameterization) ever executes under test. A regression introduced during the move silently disables or corrupts the email_domains_blacklist/whitelist spam control for every site relying on those settings, with no failing test to catch it.

[ADVISORY] The new failure-payload contract (errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: user.attributes.slice(...)) — the only bridge the client uses to populate rejectedEmails — is pinned by no test in the diff. Any later change to that response shape (renaming keys, switching to full_messages, dropping values) turns the client's duck-typed guard `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` into a silent no-op, so the blocked-email UX disappears with no failing test anywhere.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships the blocked_emails table, model, and signup enforcement, but contains no writer anywhere — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed ever creates a BlockedEmail row; only test fabricators do. Operators cannot use the feature this PR adds without hand-crafting SQL or console inserts; until a write path exists, the new query inside every signup's validation runs against an eternally empty table and the entire enforcement is dead code in production.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is a side-effectful predicate: it increments match_count and stamps last_match_at on every invocation, and it is invoked from inside User#valid? via EmailValidator, so a write fires invisibly from any code that merely asks whether an email is blocked. The model's own spec states the table exists so operators can see 'whether those emails have ever been blocked' via last_match_at — but any read-style call (an operator verifying an entry from the console, which is the only ops path since no UI ships, or any flow that runs user.valid? more than once per attempt) inflates match_count and stamps last_match_at, silently corrupting the abuse-attempt evidence the feature was built to collect.

[ADVISORY] Neither the blocked-email entries nor the lookup value are case-canonicalized: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` compares raw user input against raw stored entries with no downcasing on either side (the diff's own domain-restriction regex needs a case-insensitive flag, confirming emails are stored un-normalized). On case-sensitive adapters (PostgreSQL, Discourse's primary database), a signup using 'Bad@Spam.com' bypasses a blocked entry 'bad@spam.com' — should_block? returns false with no error, so the enforcement this PR exists to add is defeated by capitalization and the signup succeeds.

[BUG] match_count is updated via a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) with no atomic SQL increment, no locking, and no version column, and the save writes the full row from a stale read. Concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked address both read the same count and last-write-wins, losing increments — undercounting most severely during concurrent spam bursts, the exact scenario the counter exists to measure — and the full-row save clobbers concurrently updated match_count/last_match_at values.

[ADVISORY] action_type is declared NOT NULL with no column default — the default lives only in the model's before_validation, which raw SQL inserts bypass — and there is no CHECK constraint bounding the integer to the two legal Enum values. The only viable write path — the manual table load the spec comment explicitly describes ('If we manually load the table with some emails') — fails on the NOT NULL violation unless the operator knows the undocumented Enum integers (block=0, do_nothing=1), and an out-of-range value like 2 inserts cleanly and makes should_block? silently return false, disabling blocking with no error anywhere.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes every server-side email error — including uniqueness ('has already been taken') and domain-restriction failures — into rejectedEmails, whose check (lines 69-74) then displays the generic 'user.email.invalid' message while discarding the server's per-field messages, including the new user.email.blocked string this diff adds to the locale file. A user whose address is merely taken is told inline that the address is invalid (the real reason appears only in the transient flash banner), and the field-level validation never shows the actual server rejection reason the backend carefully returned in errors.email.

[ADVISORY] The only test of the new enforcement stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and invokes validate_each directly, so nothing in the diff exercises the actual User wiring (validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?), the users_controller errors/values response contract, or the JS rejectedEmails path. Inverting the gate to `unless: :email_changed?` or drifting the response field names between users_controller and the JS leaves the suite fully green while the blocked-email feature silently stops working in production — no spec fails and no code raises.

[BUG] The client-side rejection mechanism added for blocked emails actually fires for every server email error — including uniqueness ('has already been taken'), whitelist/blacklist, and presence failures — because users_controller returns `errors` for all failed creates and this code pushes any such email into `rejectedEmails`. A user whose email is already registered sees the field flip to the generic `user.email.invalid` message (persisting for the controller's lifetime, surviving modal close/reopen, and overriding the pre-validated `authOptions.email_valid` path for omniauth signups, since the rejectedEmails check runs first at lines 67-72), so the actionable reason is visible only in the transient flash and the objective silently broadened from 'blocked users' to all email-rejection classes; repeated failed submits also push duplicate entries since pushObject does not dedupe.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail feature ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, seed, or rake task exists to create blocked_emails rows — so the enforcement this PR adds is dark in production. Operators can populate the table only via raw SQL (the spec comment itself assumes 'we manually load the table'), and the migration defines `action_type` as NOT NULL with no database default (the default lives only in the model's before_validation callback), so even the manual path requires knowing internal enum integer codes and raises a NOT NULL violation otherwise; no user can actually be blocked until follow-up work ships.

[ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction logic ported out of user.rb into EmailValidator — plus the new users#create `errors`/`values` response contract and the JS rejectedEmails push — has zero tests in this diff; the new validator spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and exercises only the blocked branch. A regression introduced during the port of `email_in_restriction_setting?` (dot-escaping, regexp construction, branch ordering, or the `errors.blank?` gate) silently stops enforcing admin-configured email_domains_blacklist/whitelist restrictions at signup, and no test added in this diff fails; sites relying on those settings for spam control lose enforcement without any signal.

[ADVISORY] `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a database UPDATE (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) as a side effect of running User validation, and issues an unconditional SELECT on every save of a user with a changed email — a validation path that previously made no blocked_emails query — while ignoring the save's return value. Every `user.valid?`/save with a changed email (signup, admin edits, omniauth account creation) now carries an extra DB roundtrip, and any code that treats validation as pure (dry-runs, previews, repeated valid? checks) commits stat writes outside any enclosing transaction; concurrent signups race the read-modify-write on match_count and silently lose increments when the ignored `save` returns false.

[ADVISORY] Because `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` is declared before the email validator in user.rb, the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` gate skips `BlockedEmail.should_block?` whenever the email already has a presence/uniqueness/restriction error, so blocked emails that are also registered or domain-restricted never update match_count/last_match_at. An admin auditing blocked attempts via last_match_at (the exact use case the diff's own spec comment describes) sees undercounted, stale statistics for precisely the emails that trip multiple restrictions, and the distinct 'blocked' reason is never recorded for them.

[ADVISORY] The `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` payload is redundant — the client already holds the submitted address in `accountEmail` and consumes only `values.email` — creating a hand-maintained cross-boundary contract whose breakage is silent because the JS guard (`result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values`) degrades to a no-op when the shape drifts. A later cleanup of the users#create failure payload (renaming or trimming `values`) silently disables client-side rejection with no error or test to catch it; deleting `values` and pushing `createAccountController.get('accountEmail')` instead removes the server-side serialization, one clause of the JS guard, and the parallel `values.email` field-name coupling that must stay in sync.

[BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds the unanchored regex Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true), so the domain check substring-matches anywhere after '@' instead of matching the whole domain: an email_domains_whitelist of 'gmail.com' is satisfied by me@gmail.com.evil.org (attacker-controlled subdomain under a domain they registered), and a blacklist of 'spam.com' falsely blocks x@spam.com.au. An admin who deploys email_domains_whitelist to restrict signups to trusted domains gets accounts created from arbitrary attacker-controlled domains that embed the whitelisted domain as a prefix (register evil.org, sign up as me@company.com.evil.org against a company.com whitelist), defeating the signup restriction; the diff rewrote email validation into a 'comprehensive' validator but carried the unanchored regex verbatim from the deleted User#email_validator instead of anchoring it (\z), so it fails to prevent a bypass of the control it now owns.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? compares the raw, unnormalized email string via BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with no downcase or strip, so a block stored as bad@spammers.org is evaded by ' bad@spammers.org' (leading space, which is significant even on MySQL's PAD-SPACE collation) and by case variants like Bad@Spammers.org on any case-sensitive backend. A blocked spammer re-registers by trivially mangling the address's case or prefixing whitespace — the mangled email passes presence/uniqueness (this diff adds no email format validation, only domain/blocked checks) and the exact-match lookup misses, so the blocklist never fires; the control silently outsources case-insensitive matching to DB collation rather than normalizing in the model, and works only by accident on MySQL's default collation.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails security control ships with no writer anywhere in the diff: no admin controller, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail rows, and the spec's own comment confirms rows are expected to be 'manually loaded' out-of-band. Site staff cannot block an email address through any product surface (only the Rails console), so the spammer-blocking feature this PR introduces is unenforceable in practice as shipped — the table and match-stat machinery exist but no operator workflow can populate them until a management UI/API lands.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a committed DB write (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at via record.save) from inside User's validation pass, making model validation side-effectful. Every unauthenticated signup attempt with a known-blocked email issues a committed write (per-request write amplification from anonymous traffic), any code path that calls user.valid? — other controllers, background jobs, console — mutates blocked_emails stats without saving anything, and validation re-runs (valid? followed by save) double-count matches, corrupting the match_count/last_match_at data staff will rely on to decide whom to block.

[ADVISORY] Both examples in the new EmailValidator spec stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and neither sets SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist, so the whitelist/blacklist restriction logic this diff moves out of user.rb into validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 4-12) is executed by no test in this diff — checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, and spec/fabricators/blocked_email_fabricator.rb, none of which reference either setting or email_in_restriction_setting?. Deleting the whitelist and blacklist branches of validate_each entirely leaves the whole new suite green, so a regression in the moved code (the setting.gsub('.', '\.') regex escaping or the unless/elsif polarity) is caught by nothing the diff itself adds: the class's designated spec advertises EmailValidator as tested while site operators' domain restrictions silently stop filtering signups, with detection depending entirely on legacy model specs untouched by this diff.

[ADVISORY] The new guard `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true in every test in the diff — both spec examples call validate_each on a freshly Fabricate.build(:user) whose errors hash is empty and blocked_email_spec never invokes the validator — so the guard's false path (skip the blocked-email lookup, the match_count increment, and the last_match_at write when the email already failed presence/uniqueness) is triggered and asserted by no test. Removing the guard outright leaves the entire suite green, so the next edit to validate_each can drop or invert it with no failing test; once that happens, signup attempts with already-invalid emails stack the 'is not allowed.' message on top of unrelated presence/uniqueness errors and inflate BlockedEmail match_count/last_match_at statistics, silently changing what admins read from those columns.

[ADVISORY] The 'adds an error when email matches a blocked email' example asserts only record.errors[:email].should be_present — bare existence of some error — and never asserts the message equals I18n.t('user.email.blocked') ("is not allowed."), the new locale key this diff adds to config/locales/server.en.yml, so the pre-existing user.email.not_allowed message satisfies the assertion just as well. If validate_each adds the wrong message — for example reuses user.email.not_allowed ("is not allowed from that email provider. Please use another email address.") — the suite stays green, the new user.email.blocked key ships with nothing verifying it is ever emitted, and blocked-email users see the misleading provider-specific text instead of the plain block notice.

[BUG] should_block? persists its match statistics with `record.save` (line 16) while running inside the user's save transaction (it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each during user validation), so when the email IS blocked, user.save returns false and Rails rolls back the whole transaction, silently reverting the match_count/last_match_at UPDATE with it. Every blocked signup attempt through UsersController#create — the only production path to this code — records nothing: match_count stays 0 and last_match_at stays NULL forever, defeating the exact operator signal the model's own spec documents ("we can see whether those emails have ever been blocked by looking at last_match_at"); stats only persist for do_nothing rows (where the outer save succeeds) and for any direct user.valid? call, producing asymmetric, misleading tracking data. The specs pass only because they invoke should_block? outside any transaction, masking the rollback.

[ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table ships inert: nothing in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed — ever INSERTs a BlockedEmail row (the only writers are the test fabricator and should_block?'s internal statistics UPDATE), so there is no shipped surface through which an operator can populate the blocklist. Admins who deploy this expecting to block email addresses (the PR's stated purpose) find no in-app path to add an entry — the table stays empty and blocks no one until someone hand-writes SQL INSERTs; the only hinted workflow is a code comment in the specs ("if we manually load the table with some emails"), for which no tooling or documentation ships, and a direct SQL load must also guess the action_type integer values since no console helper or enum documentation is provided.

[ADVISORY] match_count is incremented with a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1` in Ruby followed by a full `record.save`) instead of an atomic SQL increment, and the full save needlessly re-runs presence/uniqueness validations just to bump a counter. Two concurrent validations of the same email (e.g., simultaneous signup attempts against a do_nothing-listed address, the case where the write actually survives per the rollback issue) both read the same match_count, both write base+1, and one increment is silently lost — anyone consuming match_count/last_match_at sees undercounted attempt statistics; an `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")` would be both atomic and transaction-safe.

[BUG] should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (match_count += 1 then record.save) inside a validation-time predicate and discards the save's return value, so block statistics silently drift and any code path that merely validates a User mutates blocked_emails rows. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read match_count=N and both write N+1, losing increments; a failed stats save (validation or connection error) is silently swallowed with no log; and every user.valid? probe or repeated validation of one unsaved record issues another UPDATE, so match_count/last_match_at stop reflecting actual block attempts and admins auditing the blocklist get wrong numbers.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer — no admin UI, endpoint, rake task, or seed in the diff creates BlockedEmail rows — and action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, so the only population path is hand-written console/SQL inserts that must supply an undocumented Enum integer. Operators cannot actually use the blocklist as shipped; a bulk load like INSERT INTO blocked_emails (email) VALUES (...) fails on the NOT NULL action_type constraint, and anyone hand-loading rows has no in-repo documentation of which integers block and do_nothing map to.

[ADVISORY] should_block? matches the blocked address with a case-sensitive WHERE (nothing in the signup path downcases either side), so on case-sensitive collations a case-variant of a blocklisted email is not found and the block is silently not applied. A signup for 'Spam@Example.com' against a blocked 'spam@example.com' passes validation and the account is created — the API returns success while the blocklist policy is dropped, defeating the feature for any address spelled with different casing.

[BUG] The failure handler (lines 274-276) pushes the email into rejectedEmails for every server-side email error — including 'has already been taken' and whitelist rejections, not just blocked addresses — and emailValidation then persistently reports the generic 'user.email.invalid' reason, discarding the specific server message that arrived in result.errors.email. A user whose email is valid but already taken is told inline, for the rest of the session, that the address 'is invalid', sending them hunting for a formatting error that does not exist; the transient flash showing the real reason disappears, and the blocked-specific server copy ('is not allowed.') fetched by this diff is fetched and never rendered.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails is never cleared during the controller's lifetime (the CreateAccountController singleton survives modal close/reopen, and no existing reset path knows about the new property), so a once-rejected email keeps failing validation client-side even after the server-side condition that caused the rejection is resolved. A user whose email was taken (or blocked and then unblocked by flipping the record to action_type do_nothing) reopens the signup modal in the same page session, retypes the now-valid address, and is still shown 'invalid' with no way to submit it short of a full page reload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and enforces it via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but the diff itself adds no admin UI, controller endpoint, seed, or rake task to create/manage `blocked_emails` records—only tests/fabricators mention manual loading. Also, the migration makes `action_type` `null: false` without a DB-level default, so populating the table outside Rails would require supplying the internal enum integer. This is an operability/completeness concern grounded in the shown changes, not a runtime correctness defect when using the Rails model (which sets defaults in `before_validation`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction logic ported out of user.rb into EmailValidator — plus the new users#create `errors`/`values` response contract and the JS rejectedEmails push — has zero tests in this diff; the new validator spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and exercises only the blocked branch. A regression introduced during the port of `email_in_restriction_setting?` (dot-escaping, regexp construction, branch ordering, or the `errors.blank?` gate) silently stops enforcing admin-configured email_domains_blacklist/whitelist restrictions at signup, and no test added in this diff fails; sites relying on those settings for spam control lose enforcement without any signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff ports the domain whitelist/blacklist enforcement from User#email_validator into the new lib/validators/email_validator.rb (including email_in_restriction_setting? and the ordering/gating with `record.errors[attribute].blank?`). However, the only added tests (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and cover only the blocked-email branch; there are no specs exercising SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist behavior after the port. The finding’s concern is therefore diff-grounded as a missing regression test for nontrivial moved logic; it does not demonstrate an actual defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a database UPDATE (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) as a side effect of running User validation, and issues an unconditional SELECT on every save of a user with a changed email — a validation path that previously made no blocked_emails query — while ignoring the save's return value. Every `user.valid?`/save with a changed email (signup, admin edits, omniauth account creation) now carries an extra DB roundtrip, and any code that treats validation as pure (dry-runs, previews, repeated valid? checks) commits stat writes outside any enclosing transaction; concurrent signups race the read-modify-write on match_count and silently lose increments when the ignored `save` returns false.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (app/models/user.rb), and the new `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no prior email errors exist (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a `where(...).first` and, if found, mutates and `save`s the record (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`) without checking the return value (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This makes user validation trigger an extra SELECT (and an UPDATE when matched) and introduces side effects during `valid?`/validation runs, with a non-atomic read-modify-write on `match_count` that can lose increments under concurrency. This is a concrete performance/architecture/correctness concern around stats integrity, though it doesn’t directly break signup behavior in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Because `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` is declared before the email validator in user.rb, the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` gate skips `BlockedEmail.should_block?` whenever the email already has a presence/uniqueness/restriction error, so blocked emails that are also registered or domain-restricted never update match_count/last_match_at. An admin auditing blocked attempts via last_match_at (the exact use case the diff's own spec comment describes) sees undercounted, stale statistics for precisely the emails that trip multiple restrictions, and the distinct 'blocked' reason is never recorded for them.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. In `app/models/user.rb`, `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` is declared before `validates :email, email: true`, so presence/uniqueness can populate `record.errors[:email]` first. When that happens, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is never called, so `match_count`/`last_match_at` are not updated for attempts that also hit other email validations (e.g., already-taken email), and the distinct `user.email.blocked` error is never added in those cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` payload is redundant — the client already holds the submitted address in `accountEmail` and consumes only `values.email` — creating a hand-maintained cross-boundary contract whose breakage is silent because the JS guard (`result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values`) degrades to a no-op when the shape drifts. A later cleanup of the users#create failure payload (renaming or trimming `values`) silently disables client-side rejection with no error or test to catch it; deleting `values` and pushing `createAccountController.get('accountEmail')` instead removes the server-side serialization, one clause of the JS guard, and the parallel `values.email` field-name coupling that must stay in sync.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows users#create failure payload now includes `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, and the Ember controller uses it only here: `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`. This creates an implicit server->client contract on the presence/shape of `values.email`; if the server later trims/renames `values`, the JS guard will simply skip adding to `rejectedEmails` with no obvious failure. It’s a legitimate maintainability/robustness concern, but not a concrete defect introduced by this diff because the payload and consumer currently match and the feature works as written.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds the unanchored regex Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true), so the domain check substring-matches anywhere after '@' instead of matching the whole domain: an email_domains_whitelist of 'gmail.com' is satisfied by me@gmail.com.evil.org (attacker-controlled subdomain under a domain they registered), and a blacklist of 'spam.com' falsely blocks x@spam.com.au. An admin who deploys email_domains_whitelist to restrict signups to trusted domains gets accounts created from arbitrary attacker-controlled domains that embed the whitelisted domain as a prefix (register evil.org, sign up as me@company.com.evil.org against a company.com whitelist), defeating the signup restriction; the diff rewrote email validation into a 'comprehensive' validator but carried the unanchored regex verbatim from the deleted User#email_validator instead of anchoring it (\z), so it fails to prevent a bypass of the control it now owns.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same core flaw: the regex "@(#{domains})" is unanchored and performs substring matching after '@', allowing emails like user@evil.example.com (or user@gmail.com.evil.org) to satisfy a whitelist entry for example.com/gmail.com. This matches the golden issue about lack of proper domain boundary anchoring enabling bypass via attacker-controlled subdomains.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? compares the raw, unnormalized email string via BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with no downcase or strip, so a block stored as bad@spammers.org is evaded by ' bad@spammers.org' (leading space, which is significant even on MySQL's PAD-SPACE collation) and by case variants like Bad@Spammers.org on any case-sensitive backend. A blocked spammer re-registers by trivially mangling the address's case or prefixing whitespace — the mangled email passes presence/uniqueness (this diff adds no email format validation, only domain/blocked checks) and the exact-match lookup misses, so the blocklist never fires; the control silently outsources case-insensitive matching to DB collation rather than normalizing in the model, and works only by accident on MySQL's default collation.

adjudication.rationale: In the new model `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)`, the lookup is an exact match (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (no `strip`/`downcase`) before querying. The new `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` directly into `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and nothing in this diff shows email normalization being applied prior to validation. That makes the blocklist bypassable via case/whitespace variants on case-sensitive backends or when collation doesn’t collapse them, which is a real correctness/security defect for a blocklist feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails security control ships with no writer anywhere in the diff: no admin controller, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail rows, and the spec's own comment confirms rows are expected to be 'manually loaded' out-of-band. Site staff cannot block an email address through any product surface (only the Rails console), so the spammer-blocking feature this PR introduces is unenforceable in practice as shipped — the table and match-stat machinery exist but no operator workflow can populate them until a management UI/API lands.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds BlockedEmail model/migration and wires enforcement via EmailValidator (BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)), but introduces no admin/controller/API/rake/seed path to create/manage BlockedEmail rows. The only creation is in specs (Fabricate/BlockedEmail.create), and spec comments explicitly anticipate manual table loading. This makes the blocking feature operationally incomplete as shipped, though not a runtime correctness defect in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a committed DB write (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at via record.save) from inside User's validation pass, making model validation side-effectful. Every unauthenticated signup attempt with a known-blocked email issues a committed write (per-request write amplification from anonymous traffic), any code path that calls user.valid? — other controllers, background jobs, console — mutates blocked_emails stats without saving anything, and validation re-runs (valid? followed by save) double-count matches, corrupting the match_count/last_match_at data staff will rely on to decide whom to block.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes User email validation side-effectful: `User` now runs `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` and `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a committed write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, then `record.save`). This means `user.valid?` (and any validation pass during `save`) will mutate `blocked_emails` even if the user record is never saved, and repeated validations (e.g., `valid?` then `save`) will double-count and update timestamps, matching the finding's concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Both examples in the new EmailValidator spec stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and neither sets SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist, so the whitelist/blacklist restriction logic this diff moves out of user.rb into validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 4-12) is executed by no test in this diff — checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, and spec/fabricators/blocked_email_fabricator.rb, none of which reference either setting or email_in_restriction_setting?. Deleting the whitelist and blacklist branches of validate_each entirely leaves the whole new suite green, so a regression in the moved code (the setting.gsub('.', '\.') regex escaping or the unless/elsif polarity) is caught by nothing the diff itself adds: the class's designated spec advertises EmailValidator as tested while site operators' domain restrictions silently stop filtering signups, with detection depending entirely on legacy model specs untouched by this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves whitelist/blacklist domain restriction logic from `User#email_validator` (removed in `app/models/user.rb`) into `EmailValidator#validate_each` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb` lines 4-12). However, the only new spec targeting this validator (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts only the blocked-email behavior; it does not set `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`, nor does any other added spec reference those settings or `email_in_restriction_setting?`. Therefore, the domain restriction branches are untested by the newly added suite, making regressions in that moved logic harder to catch. This is a concrete test coverage gap introduced by the change, not a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new guard `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true in every test in the diff — both spec examples call validate_each on a freshly Fabricate.build(:user) whose errors hash is empty and blocked_email_spec never invokes the validator — so the guard's false path (skip the blocked-email lookup, the match_count increment, and the last_match_at write when the email already failed presence/uniqueness) is triggered and asserted by no test. Removing the guard outright leaves the entire suite green, so the next edit to validate_each can drop or invert it with no failing test; once that happens, signup attempts with already-invalid emails stack the 'is not allowed.' message on top of unrelated presence/uniqueness errors and inflate BlockedEmail match_count/last_match_at statistics, silently changing what admins read from those columns.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. The added `email_validator_spec` builds a fresh `User` and directly calls `validate_each`, so `record.errors[:email]` starts empty in both examples; they only vary the stubbed return of `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. The `blocked_email_spec` exercises `BlockedEmail.should_block?` itself, not the validator. Therefore, no test in this diff covers the guard-false path where an existing email error should prevent the blocked-email lookup/stat updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 'adds an error when email matches a blocked email' example asserts only record.errors[:email].should be_present — bare existence of some error — and never asserts the message equals I18n.t('user.email.blocked') ("is not allowed."), the new locale key this diff adds to config/locales/server.en.yml, so the pre-existing user.email.not_allowed message satisfies the assertion just as well. If validate_each adds the wrong message — for example reuses user.email.not_allowed ("is not allowed from that email provider. Please use another email address.") — the suite stays green, the new user.email.blocked key ships with nothing verifying it is ever emitted, and blocked-email users see the misleading provider-specific text instead of the plain block notice.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the example "adds an error when email matches a blocked email" only checks `record.errors[:email].should be_present` and does not assert the specific message/key. Since EmailValidator can add either `I18n.t('user.email.not_allowed')` (whitelist/blacklist path) or `I18n.t('user.email.blocked')` (blocked email path) depending on conditions, this test would still pass as long as *some* email error is present, and it does not verify the newly added `user.email.blocked` locale is actually emitted. This is a concrete test gap tied to the new behavior/translation, not a proven runtime defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? persists its match statistics with `record.save` (line 16) while running inside the user's save transaction (it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each during user validation), so when the email IS blocked, user.save returns false and Rails rolls back the whole transaction, silently reverting the match_count/last_match_at UPDATE with it. Every blocked signup attempt through UsersController#create — the only production path to this code — records nothing: match_count stays 0 and last_match_at stays NULL forever, defeating the exact operator signal the model's own spec documents ("we can see whether those emails have ever been blocked by looking at last_match_at"); stats only persist for do_nothing rows (where the outer save succeeds) and for any direct user.valid? call, producing asymmetric, misleading tracking data. The specs pass only because they invoke should_block? outside any transaction, masking the rollback.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `BlockedEmail.should_block?` calling `record.save` during validation (EmailValidator), but it does not show that this happens inside an outer DB transaction that would be rolled back when `user.save` fails. In typical Rails flow, validations run before the persistence transaction is opened, so a separate `record.save` would not be automatically rolled back just because the user fails validation. The PR diff also doesn’t show `UsersController#create` wrapping `user.save` in an explicit transaction. Therefore the claim that blocked signup attempts “record nothing” due to rollback is not verifiable from the diff and likely misreads Rails save/validation/transaction behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table ships inert: nothing in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed — ever INSERTs a BlockedEmail row (the only writers are the test fabricator and should_block?'s internal statistics UPDATE), so there is no shipped surface through which an operator can populate the blocklist. Admins who deploy this expecting to block email addresses (the PR's stated purpose) find no in-app path to add an entry — the table stays empty and blocks no one until someone hand-writes SQL INSERTs; the only hinted workflow is a code comment in the specs ("if we manually load the table with some emails"), for which no tooling or documentation ships, and a direct SQL load must also guess the action_type integer values since no console helper or enum documentation is provided.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `blocked_emails` table/model and wires enforcement via `EmailValidator` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but it does not add any production code path to create `BlockedEmail` rows (only the migration and test fabricators create records; `should_block?` only updates stats on existing rows). With no admin UI/API/seed/rake task in the diff to populate the table, the feature will have no effect until operators insert rows out-of-band, making the change effectively inert in normal deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] match_count is incremented with a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1` in Ruby followed by a full `record.save`) instead of an atomic SQL increment, and the full save needlessly re-runs presence/uniqueness validations just to bump a counter. Two concurrent validations of the same email (e.g., simultaneous signup attempts against a do_nothing-listed address, the case where the write actually survives per the rollback issue) both read the same match_count, both write base+1, and one increment is silently lost — anyone consuming match_count/last_match_at sees undercounted attempt statistics; an `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")` would be both atomic and transaction-safe.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the diff introduces a non-atomic read/modify/write sequence (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save`). Under concurrent calls for the same `blocked_emails.email`, two processes can read the same `match_count` and both write back `+1`, losing one increment. This yields incorrect (undercounted) `match_count` and potentially inconsistent `last_match_at` statistics. The finding is directly grounded in the new `app/models/blocked_email.rb` implementation; an atomic SQL update (e.g., `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')`) would avoid lost updates and avoid unnecessary validations/callbacks from `save`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (match_count += 1 then record.save) inside a validation-time predicate and discards the save's return value, so block statistics silently drift and any code path that merely validates a User mutates blocked_emails rows. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read match_count=N and both write N+1, losing increments; a failed stats save (validation or connection error) is silently swallowed with no log; and every user.valid? probe or repeated validation of one unsaved record issues another UPDATE, so match_count/last_match_at stop reflecting actual block attempts and admins auditing the blocklist get wrong numbers.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` the code does a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1` / set `last_match_at` / `record.save`) with no locking or atomic update (new `app/models/blocked_email.rb`). This is inherently non-atomic and can lose increments under concurrent validations/signups. The method is invoked from the email validation path (`EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), so merely running validations (`user.valid?` / `save` validations) mutates `blocked_emails` rows and can inflate/alter stats if validation runs multiple times. It also ignores the `record.save` return value, so a failed save (returns `false`) will silently skip persisting updated stats while still proceeding to return the block decision based on `action_type`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer — no admin UI, endpoint, rake task, or seed in the diff creates BlockedEmail rows — and action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, so the only population path is hand-written console/SQL inserts that must supply an undocumented Enum integer. Operators cannot actually use the blocklist as shipped; a bulk load like INSERT INTO blocked_emails (email) VALUES (...) fails on the NOT NULL action_type constraint, and anyone hand-loading rows has no in-repo documentation of which integers block and do_nothing map to.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the BlockedEmail model/migration and wires it into email validation (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) but does not add any admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed code to manage/populate blocked_emails, so operators can’t use it through the app as shipped. The migration also sets `action_type` to `null: false` with no DB default (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb), so bulk loading via raw SQL like `INSERT (email) ...` would fail unless `action_type` is provided. However, the finding overstates that the only population path must supply an undocumented enum integer: the model has a `before_validation :set_defaults` that sets `action_type` to `actions[:block]` (app/models/blocked_email.rb), so Rails-level creation without `action_type` will work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? matches the blocked address with a case-sensitive WHERE (nothing in the signup path downcases either side), so on case-sensitive collations a case-variant of a blocklisted email is not found and the block is silently not applied. A signup for 'Spam@Example.com' against a blocked 'spam@example.com' passes validation and the account is created — the API returns success while the blocklist policy is dropped, defeating the feature for any address spelled with different casing.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (no `downcase`/`lower(...)`), and `EmailValidator` passes the raw submitted value through. With a case-sensitive comparison (e.g., typical PostgreSQL text equality), a blocked record for `spam@example.com` will not match a signup value like `Spam@Example.com`, so the validator won’t add the `user.email.blocked` error and the block can be bypassed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The failure handler (lines 274-276) pushes the email into rejectedEmails for every server-side email error — including 'has already been taken' and whitelist rejections, not just blocked addresses — and emailValidation then persistently reports the generic 'user.email.invalid' reason, discarding the specific server message that arrived in result.errors.email. A user whose email is valid but already taken is told inline, for the rest of the session, that the address 'is invalid', sending them hunting for a formatting error that does not exist; the transient flash showing the real reason disappears, and the blocked-specific server copy ('is not allowed.') fetched by this diff is fetched and never rendered.

adjudication.rationale: In the failure path of account creation, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present (create_account_controller.js around the added lines 271-276). That covers *any* server-side email validation error (e.g., uniqueness `has already been taken`, domain whitelist/blacklist, or the new `user.email.blocked`). Later, `emailValidation` checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and always returns a failed validation with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, ignoring the specific `result.errors.email` content that was returned by the server. Because the computed property depends on `rejectedEmails.@each`, this generic “invalid” message will persist for that email for the rest of the session, even if the real issue was “taken” or “blocked/not allowed”.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] rejectedEmails is never cleared during the controller's lifetime (the CreateAccountController singleton survives modal close/reopen, and no existing reset path knows about the new property), so a once-rejected email keeps failing validation client-side even after the server-side condition that caused the rejection is resolved. A user whose email was taken (or blocked and then unblocked by flipping the record to action_type do_nothing) reopens the signup modal in the same page session, retypes the now-valid address, and is still shown 'invalid' with no way to submit it short of a full page reload.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, `rejectedEmails` is introduced as persistent controller state (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`), is appended to on failed signup responses (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), and is then used to hard-fail email validation purely client-side (`if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)) { failed: true ... }`). The diff shows no code path that ever removes entries or resets `rejectedEmails`, so once an email is rejected it will continue to be treated as invalid for the remainder of the controller’s lifetime, even if server-side conditions change. The computed property dependency `rejectedEmails.@each` further ensures the invalid state is sticky as the array grows.
